drills.q: Name the two independent axes in choosing AWS container compute, and give one example combination.
drills.a: Orchestrator (ECS vs EKS) and compute engine (Fargate vs EC2). Example: EKS+EC2 for a GPU-based Kubernetes-native inference workload.

drills.q: A team wants to run GPU inference on ECS Fargate. What do you tell them?
drills.a: It's not possible -- Fargate has zero GPU support on either ECS or EKS. They need EC2 launch type with a GPU-family instance (p/g series), on either ECS or EKS depending on their other requirements.

drills.q: Decode m7g.xlarge and state what kind of workload it suits.
drills.a: m = general-purpose family, 7 = 7th generation, g = Graviton (ARM) processor, xlarge = size tier. Suits general-purpose workloads where ARM64 compatibility is available, typically better price/performance than the Intel equivalent.

drills.q: Rank Spot, Compute Savings Plans, and Standard Reserved Instances by discount range and flexibility.
drills.a: Spot: up to ~90% discount, zero commitment, but reclaimable with a 2-minute notice. Compute Savings Plans: up to ~66%, most flexible (covers EC2/Fargate/Lambda, any instance family/region). Reserved Instances: up to ~72%, highest discount among committed options but locked to one instance family for the term.

drills.q: A new AWS-only project has no existing Kubernetes investment. What's the pragmatic default compute choice, and when should they deviate to EKS?
drills.a: ECS on Fargate by default -- zero control-plane fee, minimal ops. Deviate to EKS only for a concrete trigger: multi-cloud/hybrid strategy, a tool that only ships as a Kubernetes operator, or an existing platform team fluent in kubectl serving many internal tenants.

drills.q: You need to process 30,000 independent video files with no dependencies between them. Why AWS Batch array jobs over a hand-rolled SQS worker fleet?
drills.a: Batch array jobs give per-child retry handling, automatic compute-environment scaling matched to the array size, and a single job ARN for aggregate status tracking -- all of which a hand-rolled system has to build itself. Note the 10,000-child limit per array job means 30,000 files need at least 3 array job submissions or grouping files per child.

drills.q: Why does a warm pool cut ASG scale-out latency without keeping instances fully running and billed?
drills.a: Warm pool instances can be kept in a Stopped state, which only incurs EBS storage cost while idle -- when scale-out is needed, ASG starts the pre-initialized instance instead of booting cold from the AMI and running full bootstrap, cutting latency from minutes to seconds at a fraction of always-running cost.

drills.q: Distinguish the Spot 2-minute interruption notice from a rebalance recommendation.
drills.a: The interruption notice is a fixed 2-minute hard warning immediately before reclaim. The rebalance recommendation is a separate, earlier signal for elevated interruption risk with more (but not guaranteed) lead time, meant to let Capacity Rebalancing proactively launch replacement capacity before the hard notice fires -- the two aren't always both present with the same timing.

drills.q: ECS Fargate tasks are stuck in PENDING and never reach RUNNING. Name three things to check in order.
drills.a: Fargate vCPU/memory account quota for the region, subnet IP availability (each task needs an ENI/IP), and capacity provider strategy or placement constraints that might be unsatisfiable together. If those are fine, check the task execution role's permission to pull the container image.

drills.q: Why would you deliberately choose ECS over EKS even for a team that already knows Kubernetes well?
drills.a: If the workload is a small number of straightforward services with no need for the broader Kubernetes ecosystem (operators, service mesh, multi-cloud portability), the team's existing K8s fluency doesn't offset ECS's lower operational surface and zero control-plane cost -- the decision should be driven by the workload's actual requirements, not by sunk-cost familiarity with a tool.

drills.q: What's the difference between lifecycle hooks and warm pools in an ASG, and how do they combine?
drills.a: Warm pools pre-initialize instances so scale-out can pull a ready instance instead of booting cold. Lifecycle hooks pause an instance in Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait so custom automation runs before it's marked in-service or terminated. Combined, a warm pool instance still needs a lifecycle hook if final steps (like registering with a load balancer) must complete before it's considered fully in-service.
